Four Centroids

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: move the four dots and the three smaller triangle centres still follow the same rules.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or P, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the four boxes to show the lines that explain what you see.
Look for the math

Move any dot and the small triangle inside the big one moves too. Yet its sides always point the same way as the big triangle's sides, always stay one third as long, and its three corners always line up with the same two dots. Here is why none of that can change.

Four centres, one big triangle

Put a unit weight at each corner of a triangle. Its balance point is the centroid: add the three corners like arrows and divide by three. For the three triangles ABP, BCP and CAP this gives Ga = (B+C+P)/3, Gb = (C+A+P)/3 and Gc = (A+B+P)/3. The centroid of ABC itself is G = (A+B+C)/3.

The three parallels meet at G

Subtract G from Ga and the A and P terms cancel: G − Ga = (A − P)/3. The same holds with B and C. So the line through Ga parallel to AP passes through G, and likewise for Gb with BP and Gc with CP. Tick statement 1 to see all three dashed lines crossing at G. This is the page's first claim, and the logic test checks it on thousands of shapes.

A smaller triangle, turned around

Let J = (A+B+C+P)/4 = (3G+P)/4. Then Ga = J − (A − J)/3, and similarly for B and C: one homothety centred at J, with coefficient −1/3, sends A, B, C to Ga, Gb, Gc. Its sides are parallel and one third as long. The very same rule sends P to G, so J sits on GP with GJ : JP = 1 : 3. Tick statement 2 to see the lines from each corner to its small centroid and the line GP.

Where the midpoints come in

Let L be the midpoint of BC. Then G = L + (A − L)/3 and Ga = L + (P − L)/3, so LG : LA = 1 : 3 and LGa : LP = 1 : 3. A homothety centred at L with coefficient 3 sends G to A and Ga to P, hence GGa is parallel to AP. Tick premises for those medians. Also Gb − Gc = (C − B)/3, so GbGc is parallel to BC and one third of it; the other two sides work the same way.

One correction to the page: it says "let U be the midpoint of AG" and then claims CGb : GbU = BGc : GcU = 2 : 1. Those splits hold for the midpoint of AP, not of AG, unless P happens to be G. The conclusion GbGc parallel to BC and a third of it is true either way, as the last equation shows. The logic test confirms both points on every configuration it tries.

Try putting P right on top of A: the triangle ABP collapses, but the other two centroids and the three parallels still meet at G. Then tick all four boxes to see the whole construction at once.
